utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is case number IT-04-74-PT against Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Kenneth Scott for the Prosecution. I am joined today by Mr. Daryl Mundis, also a senior trial attorney, and also Ms. Josee D'Aoust, trial attorney, Mr. Pieter Kruger, trial attorney, and our case manager who is Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to turn to the Defence counsel. I know one of them but I don't know the others. I would ask you each in turn to spell out your name and give me the name of the accused you represent today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Michael Karnavas, K-a-r-n-a-v-a-s, and I represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Co-counsel for Dr. Prlic, Suzana Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Senka Nozica. I am co-counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am attorney Vensa Alaburic. I am Defence counsel for Milovoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Tomislav Jonjic, attorney in Zagreb, Republic of Croatia, Defence counsel for Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Defence of Mr. Pusic, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, attorney from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Slobodan Praljak, and in this case I shall be defending myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak. I would like to welcome all the parties present in the courtroom. As you know, this hearing is connected to the Status Conference and we intend to hold this hearing until 5.00. In the light of the number of questions included in the agenda for today, we will try to finish before 5.00, if possible, in order to bear in mind special requirements of the accused Praljak. Before addressing the items on the agenda for today, I would like to welcome in addition to the counsels and the accused, the staff members working in this courtroom, the registrar, the trial attorneys, the registrar, whom I'm happy to see again, and I would also like to welcome the interpreters who will be giving us a helping hand in today's hearing and the other hearings in the future. As you know, we will be working into French, into English, and into B/C/S. Today I have planned to convene this Status Conference and to address the following items on the agenda. I shall give you a list of these items I intend to address: (a) the Trial Chamber II, whom this case has been handed over to; I will address the question of the potential disqualification of the Judge of this Chamber; third point, I will state why we are holding this Status Conference pursuant to 65 -- to Rule 65 bis; then I will tackle the question of the various counsels and issues relating thereto; the situation of Praljak, who is representing himself; and the potential question of conflict of interest, which I will address in private session; then the fifth point has to do with the outstanding motions, a number of motions are currently pending, which is an issue I shall come back to at the end of this hearing; I will then address the question of disclosure of material pursuant to Article 66 and 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; sixth point -- issue, I will address the schedule, and I shall turn both to the Prosecution and to the Defence because I expect to have deadlines set for the submission -- for their submissions; point 8, I shall address the directive and the number of words to be used in the motions; point 9, I will specifically address the issues relating to 65 ter (E) pertaining to the pre-trial brief, list of witnesses, list of exhibits to be filed by the Prosecution; and if we have enough time, I would like to address the questions pertaining to the trial itself. I am sure there will be a number of questions raised, given that this trial has six accused. This is the first time in the history of this Tribunal -- it is the first time that so many accused are being tried at once, and it is the first time there are so many Defence counsels. These are the items on the agenda. You know that as a Pre-Trial Judge today I shall be tackling all these issues from beginning to end, which explains why there has been no meeting with the senior trial attorney of the Chamber before this hearing. Pursuant to the conclusions of the working party established by this Tribunal, in order to expedite the trials, the working party concluded that the Pre-Trial Judge must be involved in the preparation of the trial and, if possible, this same Judge should do the work of a senior trial attorney. I, therefore, wish to manage this trial from beginning to end so that this can be prepared in the best manner possible. I also indicated that I was going to address the status of Trial Chamber II. As you know, initially this case had been referred to Trial Chamber I, and it's only recently that the Judge presiding over Trial Chamber I seized this Tribunal for the case to be re-assigned to another Trial Chamber. Under these conditions, Trial Chamber II has been designated, and Judge Agius, presiding over Trial Chamber II, appointed me to be the Judge to preside over this Trial Chamber. Trial Chamber II comprises four permanent Judges, and Trial Chamber II should operate with three permanent Judges, because each Trial Chamber, normally speaking, has three permanent Judges sitting and not four. So in the next few days one of the permanent Judges will probably be re-assigned to another Chamber. The second issue pertaining to Trial Chamber II is that on the 17th of November, there will be new elections held to appoint a President of this Tribunal. I would like to make this announcement today. As a President, I have applied for this job. Another Judge has also applied for the job. And depending on the outcome of this election, if I am appointed President of this Tribunal, I will not be able to preside over this Chamber because a President is -- can only be an appeals Judge. If that is not the case, I shall preside over this Chamber and this trial. In the case I am not elected, I shall then dedicate all my time to the preparation of this trial. If I preside over this Chamber, I will have on either side of me two ad litem Judges which will be appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. These will be the Judges sitting in this trial. The appointment of ad litem Judges can only take place once a date has been set for the commencement of trial. The second point I wish to address today has to do with the question of disqualification. Let me tackle this right now. It so happens that I have been the confirmation Judge in this case, which is by pure chance. Having confirmed the indictment, the question may occur, in other words, am I entitled to preside over the Chamber that is going to be handling this trial? The Rules of Procedure and Evidence is particularly clear on this point. Let me quote Article 15(C). Article 15(C) stipulates as follows: "The Judge of a Trial Chamber who reviews an indictment pursuant to Article 19 of the Statute and Rules 47 or 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence can be sitting as a member of the Trial Chamber for the trial of that accused." This Rule, therefore, answers the question. Why was this Rule drafted in such a way? As you know, there are not that many permanent Judges in this Tribunal and there are a number of cases being tried. So the Tribunal could not operate properly if the confirmation Judge could not also be the Judge presiding over a Chamber. The bureau of this Tribunal on the 28th of March, 2003, rendered a decision pursuant to Article 15(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence pertaining to disqualification of Judges. The accused Galic had filed a motion to disqualify Judge Orie of the Galic case because Judge Orie had confirmed an indictment against Mladic, and therefore he could no longer deem to be impartial. The -- Galic had stated that there could be a risk of contamination between the two cases. The two accused in these two indictments overlapped. This was the legal argument submitted by the accused with a view to disqualify a confirmation Judge. In its decision, the bureau stipulated that if an indictment is to be confirmed, it is important to bear in mind the evidence provided that a reasonable trier of fact could reasonably conclude that to declare the accused guilty beyond any reasonable doubt. The bureau indicated that a verdict is quite a different thing. It is a matter of determining in the light of all the material provided by the Prosecution whether the Prosecution has in fact established the guilt beyond any reasonable doubt of the accused. The bureau has therefore established a clear distinction between the confirmation phase and the judgement phase; these are two quite different things. The bureau in its decision stipulated that these two decisions, i.e., confirmation or finding of guilt or acquittal, require two different approaches to evidentiary material and resort to two different systems. Confirmation of an indictment does not cause any prejudice to the guilt of an accused. To sum up, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides for the possibility of a confirming Judge to preside over the Chamber at trial. The confirmation of an indictment is only a temporary part of -- a small part of the proceeding, and the potential guilt of an accused only points to the material evidence provided by both parties in an indictment that has been confirmed. The evidence is only provided by the Prosecution as the Defence, by definition, does not state its material. As you know, pursuant to Article 15(B), any party can seize the President of the Chamber for deferral. Any request for deferral based on the fact that the same Judge has been a confirmation Judge and the Judge of the Trial Chamber will -- will be rejected by me on reading the summary to be provided in that case. Before opening this hearing, I felt it necessary to spell this out so that people don't waste any time on this. As far as I understand this, the commencement of trial has been scheduled for the beginning of February, the year 2006. As Judge Liu of this Tribunal stated, he had been seized of a disqualification motion and rendered a decision, according to paragraph 19, and I quote what he had said, and I fully share his view. This is what he said: "I therefore urgently ask the parties to use their right to file a motion before the Chamber to avoid any delaying of the proceedings." I also invite the parties to address this with the greatest caution, and before concluding on this point, I would like to turn to either party and ask them if they have any comments to make. The Prosecution, do you have any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Rule 15 is quite clear on its face, and we would have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence counsels, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, thank you, Mr. President, for bringing this up. I think it is an important point. I think the rule is clear. I believe the Galic case sort of settled the law. Galic I think was somewhat different, as the situation is now, in that the rule seemed to be amended after the confirmation of the indictment process, and I believe that was one of the issues, but that's no longer an issue, and that's not an issue in this case. From a personal standpoint, I am confident that you will be able to make the distinctions as you've already pointed out, knowing that the Prosecution only gathered the evidence and presented the evidence which it believes, and coming from your only good position, you know we don't have an investigator judge who is investigating for both sides and presenting exculpatory information. So in light of that, I'm confident that there's no need to file any motions on behalf of Dr. Prlic with respect to this particular issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Pusic for the record states today that it will be making no motions. We have no objections or comments to make, and we agree with what Mr. Karnavas said a moment ago, following what you yourself said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you want to hear all our views individually, I fully agree with the position taken by Mr. Karnavas and my colleague Mr. Ibrisimovic, and the defence of Mr. Bruno Stojic will not object or file any motions in that respect . I should like to associate myself with my colleagues and state that the fact that you, Your Honour, have confirmed the indictment does not bring into question, and I doubt that you will be unbiased in presiding over this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Valentin Coric Defence agree can associate itself with what the Defence of Mr. Prlic have just said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no reason for me not to join the other Defence counsel on their position with regard to this, nor do I object in any way to what has been said so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I would like now to address a third item on this agenda, the reason why we are holding this Status Conference today pursuant to Rule 65 bis with a view to preparing the trial. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence state that a Status Conference should be held every 120 days to enable the exchange between the parties and to seize the Judge of any potential issue. This is why I wanted this hearing to be held today. I felt it was important to get to know you because I'd -- there were a number of counsels I didn't know and it's the first time I meet Mr. Praljak. I would now like to address the issue of Defence counsels. As part of this is confidential, I would like to ask the registrar to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall resume this hearing in public session. We were formally in private session. Now, pursuant to our agenda let's turn to item 5, i.e., pending motions to date. There are several pending motions for which a solution is to be found shortly. Let me just tell you what this is about. I'm sure you have realised at the time this case was re-assigned from Chamber I to Chamber II, Trial Chamber I rendered decision on motions which were not to be settled by Trial Chamber II; and Trial Chamber II is seized of four motions which I shall address. The first motion -- let us please move into private session again. It's for a short period of time, but it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: The third motion, third pending motion, is a much more complex matter. This has to do with the question of adjudicated facts and agreed facts. As you know, in law, Article 65 ter (H) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence stipulates that when the parties agree on a number of facts, these are deemed to be agreed facts, and this saves time. Rule 65 ter (H) spells this out. It is indicated that the Pre-Trial Judge shall record the points of agreement and disagreement on matters of law and fact. In this connection, he or she may order the parties to file a written submission with either the Pre-Trial Judge or the Trial Chamber. In addition to this possibility, Article 94(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence on judicial notice states as follows: A Trial Chamber may, proprio motu, after hearing the parties, may decide to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts of documentary evidence from other proceedings of the Tribunal relating to matters at issue in the current proceedings. This Rule, 94(B), is interesting insofar as material which has been presented in other proceedings, materials over which a final judgement has been rendered can also be used. This means that judicial notice can be taken of these facts. In the light of this, if the Prosecution filed a motion on the 4th of April, 2005, to request to begin with the admission of 514 [as interpreted] facts which had been admitted in other proceedings, Furundzija, Alesovski, Kupreskic, Blaskic, Kordic and Cerkez, Naletilic and Martinovic. After this motion was filed, the accused Petkovic and Prlic filed on the 18th of April, 2005 their reply, and on the 25th of October, 2005, the Prosecution sought leave to file a response. The 27th of October, 2005, the Prosecution filed a new proposal and asked that the 514 facts, with the exception of nine of them, be admitted. On the 7th of November, 2005, in other words yesterday, I received a fax relating to this matter. The Defence counsel have filed their reply and concluded that the Prosecution must amend its conclusions, otherwise no agreement can be reached. This is an important matter if the trial is to unfold as appropriate. Obviously, if there is judicial notice of a number of facts which are not challenged, this will mean that some witnesses will not have to come, witnesses which otherwise would have come to testify about these various issues. The Prosecution had filed its motion and included 14 main points. The historical background of the conflict, the conflict of the Vance-Owen Plan, the 15th of January ultimatum, Gornji Vakuf, the April -- February to April 1993 Vance-Owen Plan, Herzegovina 1993, Sovici-Dojani [phoen] settlements, Mostar, the Heliodrom, Lusabuski [phoen] prison, Vares, Stupni Do, so on and so forth. So there were 14 items listed, and in a schedule the Prosecution listed items which had been divided by those 514 facts, nine of which had been taken out. Now, following the response and reply by Prosecution and Defence team respectively, the Prosecution had prepared a chart and stipulated that on a number of facts there had been an agreement on the part of the Defence counsels. The Defence counsels challenged this. This table which had been prepared by the Prosecution was in the schedule of the submissions presented on the 25 -- 27th of October, 2005, and this provided, (a), a list of facts; (b), the accused, Petkovic, Coric, and Pusic; and then one heading for Prlic and Praljak. I realise that one of the accused was not listed on this chart, and based on this the Prosecution had then drawn up -- let me randomly turn to point 115. Item 115 has been accepted by the Prosecution and by the Defence team. This table was then challenged on the 7th of November. And on the 7th of November in the written submissions which were filed by Petkovic, I noticed that the Defence team challenge the acceptance of 41, 55, 65, 61, 79, 139, 140 -- correction, 55, 64, 65, 71, 79, 139, 140. So this has been challenged. We will then have to move on as follows. An agreement has to be reached between the parties, and this has to be done in two stages. I would like to ask the Prosecution to contact the Defence counsels in order to -- the Defence counsels and Mr. Praljak, who is representing himself, we should not forget him, and -- so that you prepare a definitive list of those agreed facts which we knew. If out of these 514 facts you still wish -- you still want some of the facts to be admitted because they are challenged, you then -- in the second stage, I recommend you do as follows. The Defence team should indicate on a point-by-point basis the reasons for which it does not wish to admit the fact in question. The -- so that the Trial Chamber can determine the matter and be fully informed. In a nutshell, the Prosecution, the Defence teams, and Mr. Praljak need to get together and prepare a definitive list and consolidated list of those facts that have been accepted by both sides; and secondly, if the Prosecution -- if an agreement is not reached with the Defence, wishes to have some facts admitted by the Trial Chamber, then the Prosecution is to file a motion and submit it to the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution should then state point-by-point why it disagrees and the Trial Chamber will determine the matter. By and large, this is how we shall proceed. Before moving on to the next item on the agenda, I would like to ask the Prosecution if it has any comments to make in regard to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May it please the Court, the -- there is a rather long history to those matters as Your Honour has just recounted in part. We did indeed file a most recent submission on the 27th of October, in which we attempted to set out what we understood to be, as best we could, the respective positions of the parties. I agree with Your Honour completely that it appears based on the subsequent filing or submission made by the Petkovic Defence, that apparently there was yet still some misunderstanding. And I just want to clarify for the Chamber that apparently is all it is. Certainly the Prosecution has not attempted to misstate anything intentionally, but I think in fact what this goes to demonstrate, unfortunately, is the nature of the way this has proceeded all along. It has been one step forward and two steps back or sideways or something, but not much progress. We will persist in and do what the Chamber, what Your Honour, has directed us to do. I will point out, and I suspect perhaps if counsel are given the opportunity to address Your Honour that they will do the same. The basic procedure as to point 2 -- let me back up for one moment. As to point number 1, to clarify, for all the parties to clarify jointly those matters which are agreed, if any, at this point. I certainly agree with the Chamber, and that will be pursued immediately. As to point number -- or as you say stage number 2. As to the unagreed facts, if you will. I think, Your Honour, that essentially this process has been -- has been carried out. There have been a series of submissions since spring, one in August by the Defence, and one again more recently in which there was -- whether the Prosecution agrees with them or not, I would have to say a lengthy response point by point to the Prosecution's proposed agreed -- adjudicated facts. So I'm not sure how much further that will take us. I suspect what the Defence will say - and I don't pretend to speak for them - but I suspect what Defence will say is that they in fact have already engaged in this process and made a number of submissions over the past several months. As to any facts which are not agreed by the Defence, the Prosecution would persist, Your Honour, in submitting those adjudicated -- those proposed adjudicated facts not agreed and not withdrawn by the Prosecution. One of the fundamental points that the Prosecution has tried to make since the 4th of April this year is that adjudicated facts are not fundamentally matters of agreement, that a fact is adjudicated based on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, the fact is adjudicated whether the parties agree or not and whether a party likes a particular fact or not. It's either an adjudicated fact or it isn't. So the fact that the parties don't agree or the Defence doesn't agree, Your Honour, with all respect, does not resolve the matter. But just to quickly summarise the Prosecution's position, Your Honour, we will indeed communicate with the Defence on identifying, if any, those facts on which there is agreement. And then we will indicate -- I indicate now that we are -- we will persist in all the remaining facts except for those that we have in fact expressly withdrawn. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now turn to the Defence counsels, and I shall give the floor to Mr. Praljak, if you would like to say something, Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor first and then we shall hear the Defence counsel. So you have understood what all this is about, Mr. Praljak, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Adjudicated facts can be taken as adjudicated facts if all the circumstances had been taken into account at the relevant time. Having followed trials for a long number of years, it seems to me that it was proceeded in the following way, that an individual, small part would be taken and then the entity would be looked at. Not all facts were taken into account, but small bits of a broken mirror were looked at, and this is something which is wrong. That is what leads to war since the days of the ancient Greeks. As for my two Defence attorneys, who are not with me now, I was not prepared to agree to any fact that was not based on the totality of what was going on in the territory of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the former Yugoslavia. That is why I request that the Court do the following because this case is more general than the previous cases. Regardless of whether we are talking about Milutinovic, or Cerkez, or Blaskic, or somebody else, our indictment is quite different. As I've already said, it goes back to the very inception of the war and its production. So I am not prepared to accept the position of any individual man or his commission or non-commission can shed light on what I did during that war. That is why I'm going to ask that all relevant facts be taken as a point of departure. We made a great effort to explain everything that concerns this war, its political part, its military part, its humanitarian part, and especially the activity of the Croatian state in all of this. The wounded, refugees, humanitarian assistance, the arming, for which I claim that we do have facts, that not a single state in the history of mankind behaved in that way when aggression was committed against it. For example, a fact has not been dealt with sufficiently from the point of view of science. For several years, Croatia had over 700.000 refugees, and if you look at the United States, for instance, and if you look at the proportions involved, that would mean as if the US had taken in 43 million refugees. If we were to look at Italy, for instance, that would be 16 per cent of the population, the total population, that is to say, 16 per cent of 50 million people, so that is 7 and a half or 8 million refugees. And then the social system had changed, a third of the territory was occupied, there were terrible problems involved. The situation was even worse in Bosnia-Herzegovina because a state disintegrated within a single day. From all the different points of view that are characteristic of a civilisation. That is to say, all law and order collapsed. There was nothing. There was no police, no water, no electricity, no nothing. So we can only reach the truth if we look at all the general facts and if we look at what each individual could have done, not what we would expect an individual to do with an attributes of a god. That is the only way in which we can deal with this. I am not going to agree with the decisions that were made in cases that were much less broad than this particular case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could supplement what I believe Mr. Praljak indicated, which is exactly our position, which is in the previous cases you didn't have the depth in those indictments as you have in this particular case. There wasn't issues of the joint criminal enterprise, as it's stated in this particular case. And for whatever reasons, the lawyers in those cases may or may not have decided to challenge certain issues or to address them in whatever fashion they wished to do so based on their theory of the Defence. Having said that, I just want to point out a couple of points. First, with respect to adjudicated facts, as the Prosecution has acknowledged, we have spent a tremendous amount of time working on these adjudicated facts and tried to find a way of bridging the gap. We submitted lengthy responses. Initially there were some complaints that we were too pithy in our responses. We then went back and we spent more time. I don't expect the Prosecution to agree with much of our positions, but nonetheless we satisfied their appetite for having more -- more facts as to why we couldn't agree to certain adjudicated facts. Certain adjudicated facts are just plain and absolutely wrong. And with all due respect, Your Honour, Courts do make mistakes. Even appellate courts make mistakes; it's just a fact of life. And so there's some facts you can point out scientifically that they're absolutely wrong. We cannot accept. Others are taken out of contest context, a matter which Mr. Praljak pointed out quite aptly and eloquently, might I add. There are other issues that we believe were not fully addressed. What we have tried to do is to amend certain adjudicated facts, so then they become agreed facts. The Prosecution, or at least some of them, don't like that idea. Frankly, I think it's better because then if it goes to an agreed fact, it's stipulated, you take judicial notice, it's not subject to a rebuttable presumption, it's the end of the case. So I think to the extent that we can agree on those adjudicated facts, even if we have to tweak them a little bit, or a lot, as the case may be, I think it's best for everybody. I don't suspect that we're going to go far beyond the point where we are. I think all parties have dug in at this point with respect to adjudicated facts. It might be helpful with Your Honour to sit down with all of us and we can go through every one. It may not be the most useful consumption of your time, but I think the only other solution might be for you to make a decision. But I think the parties, at least with respect to the adjudicated facts, have stated quite clearly and have articulated their points to the point where a decision can be made. Frankly, I think we need to try this case differently from the previous cases because in those cases you didn't have the issues that you have today. And in this particular case, the president of the Republic of Croatia, President -- the late President Tudjman, is being tried in absentia, in essence. And so is Susak, so it Boban, so is Bobetko, so is everybody else, in the sense when you look at it you have a joint criminal enterprise which entails the entire Republic of Croatia along with members of the HVO and so on and so forth. In light of that -- and we have -- and since those trials, might I add, we have a significant amount of new material that wasn't available to the lawyers. For whatever reason some archives were not available, now they are. So we have to look at the case from a different perspective. And I understand there is this completion strategy, but frankly when my client is looking at spending the next 20 years in prison, I care little. I am deeply unmoved with all due respect to the UN's completion strategy. That's their problem. They've decided to have a court, they've decided to indict, they've decided to have this comprehensive indictment. And so now they shouldn't -- the Prosecution especially shouldn't expect me to roll over and agree to everything so that we can just go straight to sentencing. And I've stated this privately and I'll state it again publicly. If we were to agree to many of those facts that they're suggesting, then there's no sense in having a trial. And I speak for both the adjudicated and the agreed facts. With respect to the agreed facts, again if you look at them and we did answer those questions -- we did answer most of them I believe with some specificity. We are willing to do so again. It takes a lot of time to get all counsel together. Lead counsel for one of the accused has yet to come, and previously there was a dilemma in that particular case. Mr. Praljak now is going to be defending himself. Somehow we are going to have to manage to get all together. But I think that with a short deadline that you might wish to impose upon us, otherwise we tend to be working on other matters that are equally as pressing, we can try to present more facts or more reasons as to why we cannot agree with certain proposed agreed facts, which in essence have been lifted wholesale from the indictment. When you look at it -- when you look at it as a whole, Your Honour, and I don't mean to be disrespectful to the Prosecution, but when you look at it they're really overreaching, and they really don't want to have a trial. They want to have a sentencing. That's what it looks like. Now, I might be overstating their case, but maybe they want a short trial, but they surely don't want to have a whole lot of defence in this particular case. And that's why, and I don't mean to be flip about this, but that's why I don't think that we're going to be able to agree on a whole lot. To the extent that we are able to find some points hat we are willing to agree on, we've indicated those. Beyond that, I have to be honest and I have to be candid, and I try to be whenever I'm speaking to the Court. I'm not so sure I'm going to go beyond I'm not going to be able to go beyond what I've already done because my first submission was an honest one based on the realities of knowing that you would have to make a decision. But I'm willing nonetheless to show the flexibility, to go back, and to do the very best I can - I know my colleagues will do the same - to see how we can bridge this gap. And I think it would be good for all of us to meet with the Prosecution. I certainly have no objection to that. But again, I don't want to sound like a Cassandra, but I would not be expecting too much, Your Honour, with the greatest respect. I'm just kind of forewarning you that we're going to do the best we can, but there's not a whole lot of room that either side is willing to give on these issues. And I want to go back and I want to commend Mr. Praljak for his eloquence in stating the obvious, which is that in this particular case the way it has been charged, the indictment, and when you look at all those permutations in the indictment, when you get to paragraph 17 - it's what I call the smorgasbord approach - of charging in every conceivable way, for everything, when you look at that and you have to keep that in mind, Your Honour because -- and one other point I want to make before I forget. In the previous 65 ter we had a particular issue with respect to the reading of the indictment. What is not in the indictment is part of the charge. For instance, one minor issue, or major, depending on how you look at it, are the events in Ahmici. We're told that that's not part of the indictment that I don't have to defend. But at the same time the Prosecution says that they're perfectly -- it's perfectly acceptable for them to use those events in order to draw certain conclusions. That's fair. That's their point. But I need to know what is it in this indictment that I have to defend. If it's the four corners of the indictment, that means every single word. Now -- coming from the continental system, I'm sure you appreciate that that's what I have to do in this particular case. So when you put something in the historical background that later on the Prosecution will be able to use that historical background in order to lay a foundation for a conclusion which they wish you to arrive at, that means that I need to attack that very foundation if I believe that foundation is not true and complete. And that's where we're going to get into some problems, and that's why we're having difficulty agreeing with everything that the Prosecution wishes for us to agree on. Because if it goes unchallenged, I will then be reading it in the judgement and it's an admission that I have made on behalf of my client, and in essence what I'm being put in is that very difficult position of where I'm having to agree to a fact in order -- so we can have quick proceedings while at the same time I am putting my client in jeopardy. And that's why these agreed facts are not something to be taken lightly. And that's why, Your Honour, I believe that you cannot expect from us too much on that. That's our position, and I'm sure my colleagues will chime in if they have a different position or if they want to supplement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't wish to add to anything that Mr. Karnavas has already said at this point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am very pleased to have had Mr. Karnavas, who defends the accused, to present his client's views and position and ours, too, and I fully endorse what he said with respect to our policies. And I think that we should all state our views and stress that the Defence will not by any move or step contribute to the realisation of the closing-down strategy, unless it contributes to the quality of the defence of each of the accused. So we're not in favour of the completion strategy unless it contributes to the quality of the defence. And I think that it is very unjust to expect the Defence by -- or intimating to the Defence that it would be good to align itself with the factual, undisputed facts of the case and the positions or function of each of the accused therein and that all that remains for us to do is to set up the links between the crime and the perpetrators of the crime and present evidence which would influence weighing up of the sentence itself. Mr. Karnavas explained that the Defence will not agree to endeavours of this kind and that we'll do our best and give our all to prevent this trial from following along those lines, and therefore adjudicated facts as a subject matter is very interesting. I'm going to continue speaking about specific features and indicating the following. Whatever the further discussions about adjudicated facts take in the form that they have been presented and proposed I consider to be unproductive, and I believe that on the basis of a proposal of that kind that has been made, we're not going to arrive at the proper results. In our motions and filings, we tried to indicate and show that the Prosecutor presents as an adjudicated fact whole paragraphs from the indictment, adjudicated fact as in the singular, and with one example, and fact 142 in fact, I show that in that proposal there were 13 facts in fact and one value judgement. Therefore, I consider that the Prosecution should be guide in the following way. If through their proposals they wish to establish the facts which were adjudicated ones, that their proposals should be dovetailed with a court practice here in the Tribunal, case law, and that each fact should be a fact in the singular and not have proposed value judgements or legal characterisations. I think that only on the basis of adjudicated facts formulated in that way we shall be able to make a step forward and truly coordinate our positions according -- on something that the Defence considers to be acceptable as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Valentin Coric Defence counsel would like to support what my colleagues have said and I would just like to add a few sentences. There is a technical problem, and I would like to say this. Correspondence on this matter, you and other colleagues have mentioned this and it could be enriched further in view of the fact that I'm not the sole Defence counsel who in recent weeks has been receiving mail very irregularly. And I established today, or rather, this morning that I found in my locker 10 to 15 filings that I had not previously found there. So I established this problem two weeks ago and I managed to deal with -- to settle that problem by corresponding with the registry. However, it appeared that many more documents had been sent that -- more than the number I found. So maybe if we receive some documents later on, belatedly we will be responding to that. That is a technical point. But what I consider to be far more important is the following. All the adjudicated facts proposed by the Prosecution stem from the judgements made which cannot be considered to be in force at present. We all know full well that the Martinovic/Naletilic case has still not been finalised, the appeal has still not come in. And another point with respect to adjudicated facts come from the Lasva Valley cases, and from the Croatian media and Bosnia and Herzegovina media it has become common knowledge, or rather, guesses and speculations have been made that the Prosecution ask for a revision or re-trial in one of those cases. Now, the Prosecution has not denied statements of that kind that have appeared in the press, so we have to take these speculations seriously and the possibility of that kind of confidential material actually existing. Now, if it does turn out that in one of the cases of the Lasva River Valley trials that we have a repeated trial in view of the fact that all those cases are closely linked together and the domino effect is present, it remains to be seen what the judgement will be and how it will reflect on the other cases in the Lasva River Valley. In other words, I don't think that it would be too extensive to conclude that at this point in time it is too early to decide about adjudicated facts, or rather, facts that the Prosecution considers to be adjudicated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down for the benefit of one and all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, apart from the comments that my colleagues have presented, we have nothing further to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Prosecution, let me outline two major points from what has just been said by Mr. Praljak and various Defence counsel. First it has been referred to, Naletilic/Martinovic case that is currently on appeal. So here we indeed are faced with a problem because only facts that have been adjudicated finally can be admitted. That's the first hurdle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: What can the Prosecutor tell us about these two legal issues I've outlined? First of all, the matter of potential revision of a judgement, of an Appeals Chamber judgement? And secondly, the Naletilic/Martinovic case? Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would ask to go into private session at this time before I address these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier on, the Naletilic/Martinovic case was mentioned. According to the Defence, this case is on appeal and the facts should not -- such as 271, 272, 273, all these facts should not be in the list. There are a number of facts pertaining to that case. I now turn to the Prosecution. What can you tell us about the Martinovic/Naletilic case in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you'll allow me, when I responded to the Chamber's first instructions on this some time ago now, the Chamber had given us a two-stage direction on the matter of adjudicated facts. One was that the parties should meet and indicate on which facts they can agree; and the second stage was that there be a further exchange of detailed submissions. And I have to say that when I rose to my feet some minutes ago, I specifically responded, quite specifically, only to those issues. But now I've heard counsel and Mr. Praljak go on for some time frankly addressing the merits, some of the merits of this issue. I'd like to just very briefly mention a couple of points before specifically answering Your Honour's question, with the Court's indulgence. There have been a number of statements made, Your Honour, that with all respect to counsel are simply not correct. In a number of cases before this Tribunal, for example, the existence of an international armed conflict involving the action and the control of the Republic of Croatia on the territory of the independent state of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been extensively litigated by parties who have exactly the same interest, identical interest, to these accused. And other Defence teams supported by the state of Croatia have actively litigated that issue. At least 14 Judges of this Tribunal, both in the Appeals Chambers and in the Trial Chambers have found without exception or dissent, not a single dissenting opinion, that there was in fact an international armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina involving the state of Croatia. It is one of the most frequently and actively litigated points before this Tribunal in the last 12 years. So for counsel, with all respect, to stand up and say this just isn't the same case, these issues just haven't been looked at before, is simply not accurate. The same can be said on the issue of widespread and systematic. There has been extensive findings on this case and other cases that relate also to this case on the existence of the common element of some of the charges in the case and that is that there was widespread and systematic behaviour. There has been extensive findings in these other cases that the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, engaged in widespread crimes against Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will leave it at that, but I simply wanted to address those specific points. As to Your Honour's specific question on the Naletilic case, Your Honour is correct. When we made our most recent detailed submission, I believe at the end of August, on the 29th of August, we indicated on the Naletilic facts those that we indicated may be considered on appeal, and that's the language we used. And I don't know if the Chamber -- if Your Honour has it in front of you, but I'm just pointing -- I'm just turning by example to fact 254 on page 65 of our 29 August submission. We indicated there that we thought that that fact may be considered on appeal. And we agreed for purposes of the current exercise and putting off for the moment what might happen when the Appeals Chamber issues its final judgement in the Naletilic case. But as to the moment we would consider that -- as to that kind of fact the determination of being an adjudicated fact can well be suspended. However, there are other facts, it's our position, in the Naletilic case, for example, on that same page, fact 256, which is our view, the Prosecution's view - the Defence may disagree and the Chamber may of course ultimately make its own determination - that that particular fact is not on appeal. The fact that an appeal is pending does not mean every fact in the Trial Court judgement has been challenged. So to be specific, Your Honour, as to those facts which we have indicated in our submission may be considered on appeal in connection with the Naletilic case, I agree, the Chamber can consider those, if you will, suspended at the current time. However, there are other facts which we believe are not in fact on appeal in that specific response to Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your comments. Needless to continue talking about Naletilic, I think we have rounded up this question very well. Also, we have a motion pertaining to Rule 92 bis (D), i.e., the admission of testimonies taken or testimonies in other cases. A motion has been filed, the Defence team has replied, and the Trial Chamber will be able to provide a response on this particular issue very promptly. At 20 minutes to 4.00 we shall have to make a break. So I shall try to speed things up and address point 6, i.e., disclosure of material. As you know during a Status Conference, the Pre-Trial Judge must see whether disclosure of material is smooth between the Prosecution and the Defence team. There are three important moments. Article 66(A)(i), Article 66(A)(ii) and Article 68. Can the Prosecution detail me or tell me about the various material which has been disclosed to the Defence teams and then I shall give the floor to the Defence team if there are any difficulties. The Prosecution, you may start off with 66(A)(i), 66(A)(ii) or Article 68. You may start whichever way you like. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In connection with to Rule 66(A)(i), the supporting material, of course that material was produced some time ago, and I don't think there's any dispute to that. As to 66(A)(ii), the prior statements of Prosecution witnesses, it is our position that there has been and is substantial compliance with there. There has been voluminous disclosure of those materials over the past 5 months. I say "substantial" because as new statements are taken -- I'll give the Chamber an example of that in just a moment. As new statements are taken and move into the category of a witness likely to be called by the Prosecution, then of course additional statements come subject to disclosure. But it's the Prosecution's general position that Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure is being satisfied. We do anticipate disclosing some additional witness statements in the near future. For example, as I said, some of the -- there have been new statements taken from some witnesses formally under Rule 92 bis, and those statements of course become, even though they may be in fact 99 per cent the same as the previous statements, they are in fact new statements that have been formalised by a hearing officer under 92 bis, and of course those additional new statements will have to be disclosed. As to other Rule 66(A)(ii) witness disclosure, there are some Rule 70 witnesses. A number of those have been disclosed to date, but there are others in which we are still waiting for the permission of the responsible governments or organisations whether we can disclose them or not. That is a matter that is ongoing, and we have a number of such items of correspondence outstanding. As to Rule 68(i), if you will, the actual -- so-called actual knowledge Rule 68 material. Again, we believe that we have complied and are complying with our ongoing obligations. As the Chamber, Your Honour, will be aware that is a continuing obligation, and again as additional materials are identified, they are provided to counsel, as they have been during the past several months. I think recently there were an additional 100 documents that have been identified, and we expect to be able to produce those electronically to the Defence by the end of next week. They have to be further collected, processed in terms of being put into a digital form, in a form that they can then be disclosed to the Defence, and we expect to do that by the end of next week. There again, in terms of documents there are items that require Rule 70 approvals. The Chamber may know and counsel may know that we have recently filed various submissions in other cases -- or in this case, excuse me, to receive various Rule 70 protections that some governments have asked for. That, again, is ongoing. There has been substantial work, Your Honour, in the disclosure of the non-public material in the so-called related or flip-side cases. That has been a matter which has also involved the registry, and we believe that we're approaching a point where most of that has been accomplished. I expect there will be some additional correspondence with the counsel and with the registry over the next week or two to see if we can clarify exactly where those matters stand. But as you will understand, Your Honour, that has required extensive seeking approvals and authorisations from other Trial Chambers as to what can be disclosed or not disclosed, in some instances redactions and working with the registry so those materials then can be put together and finalised for sending out to the Defence. So this is, and I think it's fair to say, and I think the registry will agree with us, that this has required a huge effort and amount of time and energy over the past three or four months but I think we're closing in on finishing that, I think. I will just say, Your Honour, and I will allow counsel to raise those matters which counsel of course wishes to raise directly. I will just say that we have in the last approximately week to ten days received a number of letters from some counsel, one counsel in particular, which has raised a number of disclosure issues, and those are in the process of either already having been addressed or will be addressed in the next days. So we believe, that's a summary, Your Honour, and that's a broad summary. I will address any specific questions the Chamber has, but that is a broad summary of where disclosure stands at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to Mr. Praljak, with regards his situation which is rather special, I would like to ask the Prosecution how it intends to disclose material to Mr. Praljak. As it stands to date, he has no counsel to represent him and there can be no disclosure electronically. Has the Prosecution looked into this matter? Mr. Scott, would you like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, as Your Honour indicates, this is a recent development. But my understanding is -- and in fact in other -- some of the other situations where counsel -- excuse me, where accused are not represented, depending on the situation, electronic disclosure is made. I suspect that a lot of disclosure is made, for instance, by CD, and CDs can be provided to Mr. Praljak, just as anyone else. And I assume Mr. Praljak has access to a computer and can look at those CDs and process them exactly the way that counsel can in other cases. As to EDS, the so-called -- the electronic disclosure system, let me be transparent with Your Honour and say I'm not entirely sure what the mechanism is. I would have to investigate that further and whether it is the policy of the ICTY -- and I say the policy of the Tribunal, I'm not talking about the policy of the OTP, but what the ICTY practice and policy is in terms of electronic access to an unrepresented accused. And, Your Honour, I'm not going to pretend to know the answer to that at the moment, but we can certainly inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one last question to put to the Prosecution before giving the floor to the accused and the various Defence counsels. Mr. Praljak does perhaps not have full command of the English language. The documents which are disclosed to him, I would like to know whether these documents would be disclosed in his own language. Will these documents be translated into B/C/S or not? Will the documents only be handed over to him in English, which means that he will not be able to make much use of them? What, in practical terms, do you intend to do? Those documents pursuant to Article 68, if there are any of this kind, how will you process Rule 68 material and disclose it to Mr. Praljak? I would like to say something on this point because this might -- may raise a serious issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Most of the material -- I would say the vast majority of it -- I'm not again going to pretend to say 100 per cent because I might make an error in making an overstatement, but the vast majority of the material that is disclosed to the Defence is provided in both English -- or let me say the original language of the document, many of them being English, but there might be an original document in Spanish or French or some other language. But typically disclosure is made in the original language of the document and also in B/C/S or the Croatian language. That is the general rule. There again, I cannot verify before the Chamber at the moment whether that's true for every single document but we can certainly look at that. As for the Rule 68 documents in particular, the practice of the Tribunal is that in most instances those documents are not translated out of the original language, but most of those documents tend to be in B/C/S in the first place because most of those documents came from either the Republic of Croatia or from Bosnia-Herzegovina or some such source, which leads them to be or causes them to be in the Serbo-Croatian language. So the vast majority of the materials, Your Honour, will be provided to the accused in the, as we call it here, B/C/S. But there probably would be some exceptions which we would have to look at specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a vast majority or a small minority are not really helpful words in a process like this. I will get all documents in a proper manner, or I will believe that my rights have seriously been infringed upon. In spite of the fact that we announced on time that I would lose my Defence attorneys because they did not wish to work under such circumstances, there was such a fuss on Friday, and I do not have the PDF key for opening documents because this is in the hands of the Defence counsel. I cannot communicate electronically. Although I have not been engaged in this line of work for a long time, I do nevertheless have a degree in electrical engineering. So when we hear these things, it's been this way, it's been that way, a vast majority, this and that, I think in this way my rights have truly been impaired in terms of a proper defence and a fair defence, and that can only lead to my not having a fair trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have been communicating on a regular basis with the OTP. I do like transparency and I like making a record. That's why whenever an issue comes up I raise it with the OTP. There is one outstanding issue which we haven't received an answer to and that was with respect to presidential transcripts. They may have more than we believe we have or that's been put on the EDS. But in any event that's one of the requests. As issues come up, I communicate. One of the major issues we have is the listing of the documents as they are put on to the EDS. If we can have that list as quickly as possible, that allows us then to, one, be on notice, and two, to -- to briefly look at what has been put on and then identify what documents we need to look at. So what I understand, and I can say I can't speak for the rest of the Defence counsel, but with respect to these sorts of issues we are getting maximum cooperation from the Prosecution. I want to commend that entire Prosecution team, so -- may be one of the few occasions where I complement OTP but this is one of them. So in any event, that's the status with respect to disclosure. Now we do understand that there are a lot of interviews that took place that are yet to be translated. Some of the witnesses -- at least it gets back to me being in the field as to who was contacted and who gave an interview and for how long. Some of those individuals seem to be rather critical for both parties to the extent that those translations could be expedited, we would welcome that. Because again, it would interfere with our ability to be ready for trial. So -- and if they could sort of prioritise to the extent possible, we would most appreciate it. Finally I just want to touch on two very brief issues. One issue is with respect to Mr. Praljak, I just wanted to note that a lot of the reports from the ECMM, almost all of them, are in English -- or they may be in another language, but all of them are in English. So that poses a problem. Also motions take time to be translated. And the second point, again, I believe as an officer of the court, which is what we would be referred to back in my jurisdiction and as a friend of this court, I would like to make an oral motion that at least for the time being the Trial Chamber can be seized of a motion to appoint the previous two counsel for Mr. Praljak on a temporary basis to act as stand-by counsel until there can be some resolution with respect to his status in how he's going to be represented and whether he will go through the whole trial without representation. I mention that for a couple of reasons. One, there is the issue of the EDS, having -- being able to access the EDS system, which I believe the record needs to be corrected on that earlier. It is rather complicated, and if Mr. Praljak is unable to access that, that's going to be a major problem. Secondly, there is the remote access to the ICTY database. Now we're able to be wherever we are and we have access to all sorts of material relevant in the preparation of the defence. Again, Mr. Praljak is going to be disadvantaged. And Mr. Praljak raised another issue that was quite relevant, and I think I need to stress that. Every accused that comes before a court is entitled to 100 per cent of his due process. So if he's only getting some or part, the vast majority or the vast minority of documents in the language which he understands now that he's going to be representing himself, that means that he's not getting 100 per cent of his rights. And I, for instance, would be offended if we were to continue in a trial where one of the accused would be receiving less than 100 per cent of his due process. And I think everyone in this room, including my brethren over there, sitting -- with the Prosecution would feel the same way, and I'm sure they probably wouldn't mind joining me in this motion, although I'm sure Mr. Scott rarely wishes to join in anything I do, but he would join at least on a temporary basis to appoint stand-by counsel, the counsel that he had to at least for the next month or whatever -- how long it takes so that there's no momentum lost. And I can assure you, knowing both those counsel, they're highly professional, they're highly experienced, they've been around on many, many cases before the ICTY, they truly believe in their client and wish to do the very best for their client. And on the other hand, Mr. Praljak has taken a very principled position, and that is he does not wish to have counsel representing him that are not getting paid. And I think that's a commendable position. And nor should they be put in a position by the UN, especially since we have, I believe, a treaty on -- against slavery, should they be put in a position where they have to endure two or three years of being in a case where they have to, in essence, work for free under some kind of penalty if they don't -- there may be some consequences legally or professionally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 20 to 4.00.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, let's resume our work. Regarding disclosure, I'd like to hear what the other Defence counsel have to say. I will now turn to you. Yes, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have been appointed co-counsel, this happened four or five days ago; Mr. Kuzmanovic as counsel; Mr. Ostojic, ten days ago. It is only today that I got my EDS password, but my colleagues informed me that for the most part there haven't been any major problems with regard to the disclosure of documents, and today I will fully join my colleagues in respect of everything that was said about these problems. But anyway, if we have any problems, we shall notify the Court in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence of Milovoj Petkovic has no objections whatsoever to the disclosure of documents via EDS or generally speaking in terms of our cooperation with the Prosecution regarding documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Valentin Coric fully supports what Mr. Karnavas said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Pusic has no problems regarding the disclosure of documents. As for cooperation with our colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor, it is more than satisfactory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As for disclosure, there aren't any major problems except for the issue of the -- Mr. Praljak's counsel, and I will endeavour to solve that problem by getting in touch with the registrar as quickly as possible. If I can't find a satisfactory solution, then I will have to make a decision in order to appoint counsel as quickly as possible in order for the trial to be fair. We have 35 more minutes, and let's now move to the main item on the agenda, the opening of the trial. According to some information I'd been given, the trial could start during the month of February. Then I received different information, according to which the trial will begin in March. We are faced with the logistical problem because when the trial opens, we'll have six accused together with their counsel and co-counsel. If we have ten lawyers plus six accused, we have 16 people. And these 16 people need to be able to sit in the courtroom, and a re-organisation of the courtroom had been considered in order to gain some space by -- and Courtroom I was to have been entirely revamped or Courtroom II. But I have no idea when the building work is going to start, and I have no idea when it's going to finish. So that's the first question mark. The second question mark is when the Prosecution will be in a position to submit its pre-trial brief. As you know - and I'm stating this for Mr. Praljak who doesn't have a lawyer, I'm telling this to him so he can follow the proceedings - according to the Rules, once all preliminary motions have been dealt with, the Pre-Trial Judge in order -- in other words, myself, must order the Prosecutor to file within a time limit that I will set and, at the latest, six weeks before the pre-trial conference that only precedes the opening of a trial by a few days, therefore the Prosecutor has to file a number of submissions. First of all, it has to file the final version of its pre-trial brief, the list of witnesses, and the list of exhibits. Before discussing this in more detail, I have one major question I want to ask the Prosecution, and that's the following: Is the Prosecution in a position to prepare its pre-trial brief? And I'd like to remind you that -- or to state that I had in my mind the date of 19 of January, 2006, as a time limit. Then the Defence would have three weeks for its own submissions to be filed, and that would mean 8 February, 2006, as a time limit. Mr. Scott, with regard to the pre-trial brief, are you faced with any problems? Will you be in a position to submit it by the 19th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe we can do that. I'm also familiar with the indications that because of the construction schedule, some of these dates may slide back, in fact, as I understand Your Honour is aware as well. But, no, the 19th of January would not present a problem for the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me now turn to the Defence. You know that first we have a pre-trial brief and it is for you to prepare briefs in response. So you would have three weeks to submit these briefs. If we set the 19th of January, then the 8th of February would be the date applicable to your submissions. I'm first going to turn to Mr. Karnavas to ask him the question whether this is agreeable to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I'm a little disappointed, I have to say, and I'll state my reasons. One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should never be disappointed, but give me your reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. By filing -- by giving the Prosecution until January 19th, it puts us in a very dangerous position from the Defence standpoint in that not only do we have to respond to that but we have very little time to really get ready to meet their initial witnesses. Logistically speaking, the case is so large, and there are so many different issues that once the Prosecution files its brief, we will have a better assessment as to at least how they intend to proceed and then we can more -- we can channel our preparation more efficiently because it's impossible to prepare for an entire case, to be ready entirely, on day one. Initially, the date was on the 20th of December, as I believe. Now, I certainly don't wish to put a burden on the Prosecution because I know that later on when I may need some concession, I'm hoping, I'm hoping, that they will give me -- give me some leeway. But I think having it so close to the trial date poses a problem for us. That being said, you know, if the Trial Chamber wishes to have those dates, that's fine. Three weeks, in my opinion, is more than enough to respond to a Prosecution pre-trial brief because I -- and I've said this publicly and I've said this on the record before, I don't think that the Defence should be in a position to outline its case because we don't have a burden of proof, but nonetheless we need to at least submit some sort of a response to the Prosecution's brief, which we will endeavour to do so. But without going into the details of our particular case, because we don't have the burden, they have the burden, that burden never shifts, and we still -- we may not even have to put on a case until after we've heard their case and after you make a ruling on the 98 bis motions. In any event, the dates are not bad, it's just that I would prefer to keep the original date of December 20th. The Prosecution -- one other point. They have a very, very large team, as I believe you may have pointed out earlier. And they've been working on this case for a very long period of time, so I don't think it would be that difficult for them to meet the original dates. But again, I don't want to put them in a position where they're being forced to hurry up on their brief. So I'm willing to show some flexibility, hoping that it will be reciprocated down the road by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I will have to join Mr. Karnavas in what he said. All the more so because objectively speaking the Bruno Stojic Defence has been properly supplied with resources just recently. So I think that this very brief deadline can be a problem. If this were to be accepted, the final date, January -- or the 19th of January, 2006, then I think that is too soon for the trial to go ahead after that, because, as I say, we are speedily going through all the exhibits that have been provided. I know that that is not a problem of the Trial Chamber; it's our own problem. But as I say, objectively speaking, we have a lot to do even by January the 19th to get through all the documents that were received by other Defence counsel in this case, so that I feel that the 8th of February would be too soon to go ahead with the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I consider that if Mr. Scott has already said that the 19th of January is suitable for him for the pre-trial brief, I should like to ask that we respect that will of his and the date, but also to take into account the needs of the Defence. And if we consider that the Prosecutor would be duty-bound to the 20th of December to submit his pre-trial brief and that we should do so by the 1st of February, that instead of the 8th of February we determine our duties towards the end of February, that is to say, the 28th of February which would make us respect the former agreement and would give us 40 days in between roughly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Valentin Coric Defence would also like to have an extension of the deadline, especially as our Defence team has come across certain difficulties in completing our team to begin with. So thank you, yes. That is my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the proposal made by Ms. Alaburic, the Defence counsel of Mr. Petkovic, is very reasonable, but of course we shall abide by the ruling of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every day gained in a situation of this kind is beneficial for the quality of the Defence, for the simple reason that the quantity of people working for the Prosecution and the resources they have is quite incomparable to what we have at our disposal, especially if the time that we have spent in my Defence, 90 per cent of that time I had to devote to seeking resources to pay for a defence team and to collect some of the enormous amount of material that exists. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I've listened very carefully. I think we should maintain the date of 19th January, 2006, for the submission of the pre-trial brief. And considering that some lawyers have only been appointed very recently, I think they should be granted at least one month between the time they receive the brief and the between -- and the time they respond. Therefore, the Defence will be able to submit its response by the 15th of February. You will have one month to respond to the brief. Let me move briefly to another issue. A directive, as you know, was issued by the president in September 2005. According to this directive, or practice direction, the pre-trial brief comprises 15.000 words. I believe that it is very difficult to abide by such a limit, but we have such a practice direction. Some exceptions can be made to the practice, of course. The first time that we have a trial with six accused. Obviously, when you're dealing with six accused you might need a different number of words than with a trial with just one accused. The easiest is to proceed as follows. If we say that 15.000 words should be the number of words for one accused, then we -- in this case we could allow 90.000 words to the Prosecution for six accused. I don't know how many pages we are talking about with this number of words. But since the indictment is quite long, I suppose that the pre-trial brief will also be a very voluminous document. I suppose the Prosecution has already thought about this problem, the issue of the number of words. What is your assessment, Mr. Scott, about the number of words?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first, Your Honour, I appreciate the flexibility that Your Honour has already shown, because indeed I think in this situation you can't really have a one-size-fits-all practice, whereas you have one-accused case and you get 15.000 words and you have six accused or ten accused and you also get 15.000 words. So I do think as the so-called mega trials begin, some of these policies will have to in fact show some flexibility. I certainly can't give an estimate. I don't know right off the top of my head what total number of words we're ultimately going to be looking at. But I had anticipated, Your Honour, frankly in thinking about this was that once we begin to get a closer idea - and I'll be guided -- I will certainly be guided by the 90.000 words - that we may seek some further guidance from the Chamber over what a page limit would be once we have a better feel for what we're reasonably looking at. But to be -- I couldn't really give an estimate at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's say that the Prosecution is between 15.000 and 90.000 words at the moment, and according to the number of witnesses and exhibits, this might change. Now, let's move to what I believe is the main item of the agenda, but we had to deal with other issues first. I'm thinking about the way the Prosecution will submit its list of witnesses and the list of exhibits. Mr. Scott, and the other senior trial attorneys for the Prosecution, please take note very carefully of what I'm going to say. With regard to the list of witnesses, in order for the trial to proceed as smoothly as possible and for the Defence to do its job properly, we need the following. With regard to the list of witnesses, the Prosecution has to apply a logic in the presentation of its case, of its evidence, and this, the logic, could be the logic we find in the indictment. In other words, first we would have background or context witnesses with possibly some expert witnesses. Then you deal or you call witnesses who will talk about the specific part of the accused -- what you charge them as part of the joint criminal enterprise. And then in the indictment we have counts of murder, destruction, devastation, and we would have fact witnesses for these -- for these items. So we need some logic in the presentation of the witnesses. We don't want to have one witness talking about a prison and the next day to move to something completely different. We need to have some rationale, some logic, and I'd like to -- you to take very good note of that and I'll be -- I'll follow that very clearly -- very carefully. For witnesses, we need to have a summary, the summary of what the witness will say; this summary should be as exhaustive as possible. Furthermore, we should be provided with very specific references to the indictment. We have a witness who will come to testify and we need to know what about. We need to have references to the indictment, to -- and also very specific cross-references to the pre-trial brief.
