This will allow the Judges to know exactly why the witness is being called, and this will allow the Defence to prepare its cross-examination accordingly. I believe that this is absolutely essential. Second point of what the Prosecutor should do is related to the list of exhibits. And with regard to the list of exhibits, we are in a common-law institution and we -- and according to me, there are two criteria related to an exhibit: First of all, the relevance of the exhibits and then the probative value. But that is to be determined, of course, by the Judges. When an exhibit is produced, the Prosecution, and then later the Defence, it's probably produced because the exhibit is relevant. You can't very well imagine the party producing an exhibit that has no relevance whatsoever. As a consequence I'm going to issue an order in the next few days, an order related to exhibits, an order to introduce the following system. We have a trial with six accused with the Defence teams that will cross-examine witnesses. As a consequence, we need to solve the issue of exhibits before the trial, otherwise we'll have objections from the Defence about an exhibit and we'll have six objections and everything will come to a standstill. I'm thinking very seriously about what we could do and I'm preparing a decision. Once you've prepared the list of exhibits, for each exhibit listed you should mention the title of the exhibit, a report, report, order; you should mention the date when the exhibit was produced, the object -- subject of the -- and then you should have a column with the reference, cross-reference, between that exhibit and the indictment; and then another column with a cross-reference to the pre-trial brief. Thus, everyone, the Judges, the Defence teams, will know very clearly that this particular exhibit is being produced because it's related to a particular witness, to a particular passage of the indictment, and to a particular passage of the pre-trial brief. Once you've listed all the exhibits, thus you can produce a schedule, a chart, with the provisional number, P -- of the exhibits, P1, P2, and you would produce an entire -- a list of the entire exhibits. These exhibits would then be admitted. Of course, when the exhibit is admitted, it doesn't mean that it is -- has been admitted finally, because it's open for the Defence to challenge the authenticity of the exhibit. But that would be a start, and the same will apply to the Defence once its turn comes. Each Defence team will prepare its own chart with a number of exhibits, et cetera. We might be faced with thousands of exhibits in this trial, so this work should be done. I will make this very specific in the order I will issue later on in order to make our work easier for everyone to be able to deal with these exhibits, because I suppose it's feasible to have a trial with thousands of exhibits, for those who are used to that sort of trial, but it might be very, very difficult for those who are not used to that sort of situation. Therefore, I would like the Prosecution to be very, very careful about this, very cautious, and submit a list of exhibits that would allow the Defence to do its job and to play its part properly. So I think there will be a consensus on this point. Once a list is prepared, the Defence counsels can then turn around and say Exhibit Number P832 is not a true document, if you are able to say so. But in order to do this, you need to have a proper list. In the few minutes we have still before we adjourn, would you like to say something? Mr. Karnavas, I think you would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly. First, I want to thank you for seeing that problem, and I totally agree. And if I may be in a position to offer a couple of pointers on -- in making that decision, Your Honour. Perhaps you could also order the Prosecutor to -- in a column to show why it believes the document is authentic and why it's reliable. So those are the three tests: Authenticity, reliability, and of course relevancy. And of course that would bind the Defence as well in introducing any documents to do the same thing. I think it's very important because we may be -- early on we may be able to agree that a lot of these documents are authentic, reliable, and relevant. But I think those two added points, Your Honour, if you could ask the Prosecutor because it goes to the foundation. Do they believe the document is authentic? And if so, is it reliable? In other words, it hasn't been tampered with. And then of course the relevancy, as you've pointed out. So if I could just -- you know, and I hate to be giving you advice, but if you could add those I would appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have no further comments? Very well. So if we can agree on this point. The Defence counsel is quite right. I think it would be advisable to have several columns on this chart. You could have the relevance column, and this would relate to a particular paragraph in the indictment. But the Defence is concerned about the authenticity and reliability of these exhibits. Of course, if we are talking about a military order with a signature and a stamp, then one has reason to assume that this document is authentic and reliable. This doesn't mean that it is not challenged or cannot be challenged. If it is an ECMM report, or if it is a report provided by an international battalion, so be it. But if you can do your job and authenticate all the exhibits which are being adduced, you have the duty to adduce exhibits which can be taken seriously. You cannot, of course, adduce false exhibits. What the Defence asks you to do is something which you would do quite naturally. I don't think this raises any major difficulties. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assure the Chamber that we will not intentionally and knowingly submit any inauthentic or unreliable documents. We may be mistaken at times because we are not perfect. But I can tell you that will never be done intentionally that we will ever submit any evidence to the Chamber that we believe is unreliable. I think that in meeting the Chamber's desire, I think what will probably be indicated in most instances will be the source of the document, which I think many times, if it's the HVO archive, if it's an UNPROFOR unit, or if it's the UN, I think if we indicate in most instances the source of the document that's going to give you the information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So as regards this particular issue, so long as the lawyers do their job and respect due process, and if the Prosecution also fulfils its role appropriately, I think this will make life easier for everyone concerned. There are a number of material issues which have not been addressed at this hearing which I do not have time to address today. But I would like to share it with you so that you can think about it, and I hope that this issue can be addressed at the next Status Conference, which could be held in the month of December, namely, the rights of the Defence after the accused -- after the accused asks questions. If the Prosecution hears a witness for three hours, how long will the Defence team have for the cross-examination? Will the Defence team also have three hours? Will each party have three hours? And Mr. Praljak, if he has no counsel, also be entitled to three hours. I hope in the meantime Mr. Praljak's counsel question will be settled. In other words, if the Prosecution takes three hours, all in all the Defence team will have 18 hours. Or are we going to approach this differently. The Prosecution has three hours and the witness is connected to one accused in particular, in that case the counsel representing that particular accused, as a lead counsel, will then proceed to the cross-examination for three hours and the other lawyers will spend less time cross-examining the witness. This is a very big issue. I have not found a solution to it yet. But we will have to come to terms with this and make sure that the trial can unfold, as it should, and in an efficient manner. Obviously if an examination-in-chief lasts three hours, the Defence team that is representing six accused people does not have to dedicate 18 hours to its cross-examination. Between you, Mr. Praljak, and I hope that in the meantime Mr. Praljak will have counsel to defend him, I would rather you agreed about this beforehand and see how this can be managed. Discuss it with the Prosecution team beforehand, please, and make sure that this is addressed properly. This might be a very complicated issue. Also, in addition to this, after the cross-examination when there are additional questions or re-examination, then what kind of replies are provided -- response is provided by the Defence? So these are just a series of questions which I have not found a solution for as of yet. If both parties can come up with a solution, and a rational solution, the Trial Chamber will be very happy. If, however, no solution can be found, the Trial Chamber will have to determine the matter. The Defence team is entitled, of course, to cross-examine any witness. That said, we shall certainly reconvene in the month of December, get together. I strongly recommend that you discuss these matters together, contact the Prosecution, and then things will be much easier. For the time being, I am presiding over this Chamber and I spend all my time working on this trial. I have just one person to assist me, Ms. Audrey Mateo. So if you have any questions you would like to raise, please contact her and talk to her. I am available 24 hours a day, but I would also like to tell you that I'm not in favour of ex parte meetings. Ex parte is not relevant. We are supposed to discuss all these matters together. I don't think that a Pre-Trial Judge should meet the Prosecution face-to-face or meet a trial attorney face-to-face either. I think everything has to be crystal clear. This is what is called a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: I'd like to thank you, and I shall let you know when we reconvene for our next Status Conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.44 p.m.
